title: Book Publishers Are Quietly Using More AI. Staff Are Revolting
key_facts: WIRED interviewed more than two dozen publishing workers, all anonymous, who say HarperCollins, Simon & Schuster and Hachette use AI tools without public disclosure or author consent.
Uses named include emailing literary agents, writing publicity and back-cover copy, designing cover art and making marketing material, using tools such as Claude and ChatGPT.
HarperCollins staff were asked to become 'AI Champions'; a current employee says leaders bought Claude licences months ago.
Agents say they suspected editors of using AI to write rejection letters and have added contract clauses barring authors' material from being run through an LLM.
Simon & Schuster staff began an open letter opposing a trial of Skan AI, a workflow-analysis tool; CEO Greg Greeley wrote on 6 Oct that no decision has been made to use it.
A Hachette spokesperson said it supports AI for operational purposes but 'does not support creative uses' including communicating with authors and partners.
Simon & Schuster's marketing chief said employees have a limited number of enterprise AI tools and use is not mandatory.
quote_evidence: But behind the scenes, at least three of the Big Five US book publishers—HarperCollins, Simon & Schuster, and Hachette—have been quietly incorporating AI tools into their publishing processes without public disclosures or author consent.

A spokesperson for Hachette says the company “support[s] the use of AI tools for operational purposes, when they help our authors’ books reach more readers,” but that it “[does] not support creative uses of AI, including communicating with our authors and partners.”
News of the open letter was published in New York magazine’s Book Gossip newsletter on October 6.
why_it_matters_hint: Authors and agents want disclosure of how publishers use AI, and staff fear job cuts.
event_date: Report published 9 Oct 2026; open letter news 6 Oct 2026
notes: Based on anonymous staff accounts; publishers' replies are partial. WIRED also says Pangram, an AI detector, indicates part of Greeley's memo was AI-written; not repeated here because detectors are unreliable.
